sections.title_en: 1. The Enactment of the Torah Reading
sections.body_en:
In addition to the mitzva of Torah study, which obligates every person of Israel to set times for Torah study every day and every night, the Sages enacted that the Torah be read in public several times a week. The Sages said (Bava Kamma 82a) that this enactment was founded following what is said (Shemot 15:22): "And they went three days in the wilderness and found no water". Moshe Rabbeinu and his disciples the prophets understood that the thirst for water was caused because for three consecutive days Israel had not engaged in Torah, which is likened to water. For just as water gives life to all living things and plants, so the Torah gives life to the soul. And since they had distanced themselves from the Torah, they did not find water. And although presumably the Torah scholars of the generation studied Torah during those three days, Israel did not engage in Torah publicly, and therefore they enacted that the Torah be read every Monday, Thursday and Shabbat, so that three days would never pass over them without a public reading of the Torah. Later, Ezra the Scribe continued to shape the enactment, and enacted that at least three people be called up and ten verses be read (Bava Kamma 82a).1

There are two main aims of the enactment of the Torah reading: the first, that three days should not pass over Israel without public Torah study. The second, that every three days they should meet the sanctified Torah scroll written in ink on parchment, according to the tradition of its writing from Sinai.

In addition, Moshe Rabbeinu enacted that on the festivals they read about the subject of the festival (Megilla 32a). And the Sages shaped the enactment when they determined how many people would be called up on each of the festivals, as explained in the next halakha.

The enactment of the Torah reading is placed on the public: every ten who gather to pray with a minyan on the days on which it was enacted to read the Torah – must read the Torah. But the enactment is not placed on the individual; therefore one who prayed with a minyan and, when they reached the Torah reading, needed to relieve himself and missed part of the Torah reading, or who was forced to leave before the Torah reading, need not look for another minyan in order to make up the verses he did not hear.2

notes_en.en: Seemingly there is a difficulty: since the Torah had not yet been given, how could Israel engage in Torah? Indeed the Maharal explained (Gur Aryeh, Shemot 15:25) that they could not engage in Torah since it had not yet been given to them, but in practice, since they did not engage in Torah for three days, they had no water. Therefore God gave Israel at Mara three important mitzvot: Shabbat, civil laws and the red heifer, so that they could engage in Torah. And one should add that the Torah scholars certainly engaged in Torah before this too, as the Sages said of the Patriarchs that they were elders and sat in the yeshiva (Yoma 28b), and Avraham's kidneys became like springs and taught him Torah (Bereshit Rabba 95:3). But they studied lofty ideas about the belief in God's unity, the service of God, the refinement of character and the repair of the world, and the public was far from this; and after they received the practical mitzvot, they could engage in Torah as a public (and see Mishneh Sakhir, Oraḥ Ḥayim 217; Mishnat Avraham on Sefer Ḥasidim 1, p. 219).

The Ramban wrote (Milḥamot Hashem, Megilla 3:1) that the Torah reading is an obligation on the public and not on the individual, unlike the reading of the Megilla, which every individual is obligated to hear. And so wrote the Ritva (Megilla 21b). And he explained that for this reason it was common for individuals to come in and go out in the middle of the Torah reading, and therefore they enacted that every person called up make a blessing (below halakha 4). And so wrote the Tashbetz Katan 185; Rav Ḥazan, author of the 'Ḥikrei Lev', in a responsum copied by his grandson R. Ḥayim Palagi (Semikha Le-Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2); and the Ginat Veradim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:21). And so wrote the Sha'arei Efrayim (7:39), and therefore if a public missed a reading – it must make it up on the following Shabbat, but not an individual (below 20). And therefore an individual who did not hear a few verses need not look for a minyan in order to hear them, as the Tzitz Eliezer (18:5) and the Yabi'a Omer (part 7, Oraḥ Ḥayim 9) wrote (and they rejected the words of the Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:23; 4:40:5, who wrote that there is an obligation to make up verses one did not hear). Moreover, some say that even one who is with the public, as long as there are ten listening to the reading, may study for himself shenayim mikra ve-eḥad targum, as brought below in halakha 12. And even those who hold that everyone is obligated to listen to the Torah reading mean an individual who is in a minyan where the Torah is being read, who is forbidden to separate from the public reading; but an individual who is at home is not obligated in the Torah reading (see Biur Halakha 146:2, s.v. 'Ve-likrot'; Tzitz Eliezer 18:5).
One who faces two options – to pray with a minyan or to hear the Torah reading: some say that it is preferable that he pray with a minyan, for the individual is commanded to pray with a minyan, whereas the Torah reading is a mitzva on the public and not on the individual (Minḥat Yitzḥak 7:6). And some say that the enactment of the reading is more important, and it is preferable that he hear the Torah reading (Halikhot Shlomo, Prayer 11:2).

sections.title_en: 2. The Number of Those Called Up
sections.body_en:
The Sages enacted that the more excellent and holy the day, the more people are called up on it (Megilla 21a; Peninei Halakha, Mo'adim 2:8). On Mondays and Thursdays, and likewise on public fast days, on Ḥanukka and on Purim, three people are called up to the Torah. What these days have in common is that they are ordinary working days, no additional (musaf) offering is brought on them, and adding people called up is liable to cause 'loss of working time'.

On Rashei Ḥodashim and on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed, four people are called up. On these days an additional offering was brought, and corresponding to it the Sages enacted the Musaf prayer, and they likewise enacted adding a fourth aliya. And there is no concern for a slight loss of working time, since on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed it is permitted to work only for the needs of the festival or for a great need, and on Rosh Ḥodesh too it would be fitting to reduce work (see Peninei Halakha, Mo'adim 11:2; Zemanim 1:7).

On festival days (Yamim Tovim) five people are called up, for on them holiness is added, which finds expression in the prohibition of work (melekhet avoda).

On Yom Kippur six people are called up, for on it holiness is added, which finds expression in the fact that even work for the preparation of food, which is permitted on a festival, is forbidden on it.

On Shabbat seven people are called up. And although in certain respects the holiness of Yom Kippur is higher, on Shabbat an aliya is added because the punishment for desecrating it is more severe, for one who desecrates Shabbat is liable to stoning, whereas one who desecrates Yom Kippur is liable to karet (Megilla 22b; see Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 6, note 2).

On Shabbatot, on Yom Kippur and on festivals, an additional person is called up, who is called 'maftir'. On Shabbatot the maftir rereads the last verses of the 'weekly portion', and on festivals he reads verses from another portion that deal with the subject of the day. The one called up for maftir reads the haftara, which is the reading of verses from the Prophet connected with what was read in the Torah (see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:7).

In the reading of Shabbat morning the whole Torah is read in order. In the time of the Talmud, in the Land of Israel they were accustomed to complete the reading of the Torah in three years, and in Babylonia they were accustomed to complete it in one year. And so all the communities of Israel are accustomed today, to read every Shabbat the 'weekly portion', and to finish the reading of the whole Torah every year on 'Simḥat Torah'.

At Minḥa on Shabbat three people are called up, because this is not the main reading of Shabbat, but a later enactment of Ezra the Scribe, "because of those who sit at the street corners" (Bava Kamma 82a). 'Those who sit at the street corners' (yoshvei keranot) are the shopkeepers who were occupied in trade on weekdays and were absent from the synagogue, and in order to make up for them the reading of the weekdays, Ezra the Scribe enacted for their sake the reading at Minḥa on Shabbat (Rashi). And some explain (Shita Mekubetzet in the name of a Gaon) that 'those who sit at the street corners' are the frivolous, and since the time of Minḥa is a time prone to drunkenness, Ezra the Scribe enacted a Torah reading, so that the frivolous would refrain from drunkenness in honour of the Torah reading (see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:8).

sections.title_en: 3. Is It Permitted to Add People Called Up?
sections.body_en:
The Sages said in the Mishna (Megilla 21a) that on days on which three or four people are called up, one does not reduce the number of people called up that the Sages enacted, and one does not add to them. One does not reduce – so as not to detract from the enactment of the Sages; and one does not add – so as not to delay the worshippers from going out to their work. And even on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed one should not add to the four called up, so as not to delay the worshippers who need to go out to their work for the needs of the festival or for the sake of an impending loss. At Minḥa on Shabbat too one does not add to the three called up, because throughout the day people were accustomed to study Torah and hear sermons, and towards evening they prayed Minḥa and went to the third meal, and they did not want to burden them by adding people called up (Rashi there, s.v. 'Ve-ein'; Me'iri).

On festivals and Shabbatot, on which five, six or seven people are called up, one does not reduce the number of people called up that the Sages enacted, so as not to detract from the enactment of the Sages. But it is permitted to add to them, because these are days on which people rest from work, and adding people called up does not cause 'loss of working time'.

And although it is permitted to add people called up on festivals and on Yom Kippur, the custom of many is that as long as there is no great need for it, one does not add people called up, so as not to cancel the difference in the number of people called up between the festivals and Yom Kippur, and between Yom Kippur and Shabbat (Rema 282:1). And some are accustomed to add people called up on them even for an ordinary need (Beit Yosef 282:2).

On Shabbat too, ideally one should not add people called up, so as not to burden the public. In addition, some hold that since today we are accustomed that each person called up makes a blessing before the aliya and after it, it is fitting not to add to the number of people called up that the Sages enacted, so as not to add unnecessary blessings (Tashbetz 2:70). However, in case of need, such as on a 'Shabbat Ḥatan' when there are honoured guests, many are accustomed to add people called up. And when the public is particular about the length of the prayer, even on a Shabbat Ḥatan one should not add people called up; only if a situation arose in which they forgot to call up one of the honoured guests, and if they do not add an aliya and call him up an insult will arise, it is permitted to add. And so it is fitting to conduct oneself ideally.3

When people called up are added, care is taken that for each person called up at least three new verses are read. Only in case of need, to prevent an insult, may one call up a person who will reread verses that were already read.4

notes_en.en:
Adding people called up on a festival and on Yom Kippur: According to many, on festivals and on Yom Kippur too it is permitted to add people called up, according to the plain meaning of the Mishna (Megilla 21a). And so wrote most Rishonim, among them: the Rambam (Prayer 12:16), Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot, Megilla 23a, s.v. 'Ḥad'), the Semag (positive commandments 19), the Rivash 84, the Me'iri, the Tur and the Beit Yosef (282:1). And so wrote the Zera Emet (3:28), the Eliya Rabba (282:5) and the Ḥida (Kisse Raḥamim, Tractate Soferim 10:6). And some say that the words of the Mishna were said only about Shabbat, but on festivals and on Yom Kippur one does not add, so as not to blur the difference in levels between them and Shabbat, and only on Shabbat is it permitted to add people called up, because there is no level above it (Tashbetz 2:70; and so it emerges from Maran). And the Rema wrote (282:1) that people are accustomed not to add people called up on festivals, except on Simḥat Torah when they add. And so wrote the Baḥ, the Levush, the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (282:1) and the Mishna Berura 6.
Adding people called up on Shabbat: According to the Tashbetz (2:70), and his son the Rashbash 429, whatever the Sages said, that one may add to those called up, is when the first blessed at the beginning and the last at the end. However, since they instituted that every person called up blesses at the beginning and at the end (below halakha 4), one should not add beyond the obligation of the day, so as not to cause an unnecessary blessing. On the other hand, almost all the Rishonim did not write this law, so that in their view the words of the Mishna, that it is permitted to add people called up without restriction, apply also when the custom is that all those called up bless on their aliya. And so people are accustomed on Simḥat Torah to call up all the worshippers (Rivash 84). In addition, if there were in this a concern of an unnecessary blessing, they would not have enacted, out of concern for the mistake of those coming in and going out, that each of those called up make a blessing (Megilla 21b). Rather, such is the enactment of the Sages, that whoever goes up to the public reading blesses for the honour of the Torah, and consequently there is no unnecessary blessing in this (Rivash 84; Ginat Veradim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:23; Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 170). And so is the custom. However, some wrote that ideally one should be concerned for the words of the Tashbetz and not add people called up without need (Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Ha-Tur 282:15; Olat Shabbat 3; Magen Avraham 1; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 6). And some added that also because of the burden on the public, ideally one should not add many people called up (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 282:3; Mishna Berura 5). And in Prague they enacted not to add more than three people called up (Eliya Rabba 282:3). And likewise when adding people called up is liable to cause chatter or to distress the public, the rabbi and the gabbaim may enact not to add people called up (see Aseh Lekha Rav 3:22). And the custom of the kabbalists of the Beit El yeshiva, according to the Kabbala, is not to add people called up beyond what the Sages enacted (Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 135:19-20). And see Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 6:6.

Some say that it is possible to add people called up while repeating the same verses, for in every reading there is study and a mitzva, as people are accustomed on Sukkot and on Ḥanukka to repeat the same verses in the reading (Rav Hai Gaon, as brought in Sefer Ha-Ittim, siman 185; Rivash 84; Shulḥan Arukh 282:2; Ginat Veradim 2:23; Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Ha-Tur 282:3, and others). And some are accustomed so ideally. On the other hand, some say that one should not repeat verses in order to add people called up, and only on Sukkot and on Ḥanukka, where there is no other possibility, are the verses repeated (Mordekhai 831 in the name of Rabbeinu Efrayim; Tashbetz 2:70). And so wrote the Rema 282:2, the Magen Avraham 4, the Peri Megadim 4 and the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 4; but concerning Simḥat Torah they agreed to permit repeating the reading according to the custom.

sections.title_en: 4. The Blessings of the Torah
sections.body_en:
Apart from the blessings of the Torah that the Sages enacted for every person to recite in the morning, the Sages enacted that those called up to the Torah reading recite the blessings of the Torah again, in honour of their going up to read the Torah in public from the sanctified Torah scroll. Through the blessing, the one called up and those listening connect to the divine source of the Torah, and because of the greatness of its subject they enacted a blessing before the reading and after it. Before the reading, the blessing is that God chose us from all the peoples, and as a result gave us His Torah. After the reading, the blessing is on the excellence of the Torah, that it is a Torah of truth and God gave it to us so that we would delve into it and innovate in it, and thereby add life and blessing to the world.

At first the custom was that only the first and the last people called up made blessings – the first recited the first blessing before the Torah reading, and the last recited the last blessing after the end of the reading, and all the other people called up would hear their blessing and thereby fulfil the obligation of the blessings.

After a time, because of the great importance of the blessing of the Torah, the Sages enacted that each and every person called up bless both at the beginning and at the end, "a decree because of those coming in and because of those going out". For the Sages were concerned lest a person come in during the Torah reading, and not hear the blessing of the first person called up at the beginning of the reading, and think that there is no blessing before the Torah reading; therefore they enacted that every person called up bless before his reading. They were further concerned lest a person go out during the Torah reading, and since he would not hear the last person called up blessing at the end of the reading, he would think that there is no blessing after the reading; therefore they enacted that every person called up recite a blessing at the end of his reading (Megilla 21b, Rashi and Rambam). And some say that the reason for the enactment is so that even one who came late to the synagogue will hear the blessing before the aliya to the Torah, and also one who went out before the end of the reading will hear the blessing after it (Me'iri there).

sections.title_en: 5. The Number of Verses
sections.body_en:
Included in the enactment of the prophets in the days of Moshe Rabbeinu, that on Shabbat, Monday and Thursday they would read – was that one person called up would read three verses, or three people called up would each read three verses. Ezra added and enacted that three people be called up, and together they read at least ten verses (Bava Kamma 82a). For this purpose one of those called up must read at least four verses (Megilla 21b).

In this enactment there is an expression of the need to contemplate the Torah with a comprehensive view. "The law of the Lord is perfect, restoring the soul" (Tehillim 19:8): it is precisely when the Torah appears in its completeness that it restores the soul, but when the comprehensive view is lost – it does not restore the soul. The number three expresses the complete idea, composed of the two sides and the centre (like thesis, antithesis and synthesis). If one of the readers erred and read fewer than three verses, he must go back and correct the reading.5

Because of the great importance of the enactment that each person called up must read at least three verses, the Sages enacted not to stop the reading at a place where there is a concern that there will be people who will mistakenly think that it is permitted for a person called up to read fewer than three verses. Let us explain further: as we learned (above 10:16), the whole Torah is divided into small sections (parashiyot), which are separated in the Torah scroll by a space the size of writing nine letters. The Sages forbade stopping the reading fewer than three verses before the end of a section, so that if a person leaves the synagogue at that time, it will not occur to him that the next person called up will read to the end of the section fewer than three verses. And likewise one should not stop fewer than three verses after the beginning of a section, so that if a person enters the synagogue then, it will not occur to him that the previous person called up began to read from the beginning of the section and read fewer than three verses (Megilla 21b; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 138:1).

notes_en.en:
When the person called up read fewer than three verses and recited the final blessing, he must go back and read properly (Maharik 177; Shibbolei Ha-Leket 40; Shulḥan Arukh 137:4). It is agreed that he must bless after his corrected reading. Some say that he should also bless before his reading (Magen Avraham 137:8; Mishna Berura 13, and others). And some say that the first blessing he recited before the mistaken reading stands for him, and therefore he should not bless before the corrected reading, on condition that they have not yet called up the next person (Taz 137:4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 5). And so one should conduct oneself, because in a doubt about blessings one is lenient.
If the person called up after him has already begun to bless, and they remembered that the previous one read fewer than three verses: on a weekday, when one does not add to three people called up, the one in whose aliya the mistake occurred should remain by the bima, and afterwards he should go up again with a blessing before the reading and after it, and they should read for him at least three verses. But on Shabbat, when it is permitted to add to those called up, they should add another person called up who will read at least three verses (Magen Avraham 137:8, and see Mishna Berura 13).

sections.title_en: 6. Ten Verses
sections.body_en:
As we learned in the previous halakha, Ezra the Scribe enacted that whenever the Torah is read, at least ten verses be read (Bava Kamma 82a). The number ten expresses an idea that appears in complete form in the world. Therefore the whole world was created with ten utterances. The minyan required for every devar she-bi-kedusha also includes ten people (Megilla 21b). That is to say, three verses express a complete idea, whereas ten verses express the complete appearance of a thing in the world, which has both an ideational side and a practical side.

Only once a year, on Purim, when the portion 'Va-yavo Amalek' is read, only nine verses are read, because the whole matter, in terms of its content and in terms of the order of the day, ends in nine verses. And there is a hint in this, that as long as there is Amalek in the world, the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, still cannot be revealed in completeness, and even our Torah reading is reduced to nine verses. (According to the custom of those of Sephardi origin the last verse is repeated, and according to the custom of those of Ashkenazi origin it is not repeated; Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 15:14.)

If on an ordinary day they erred and the three people called up read only nine verses, they have fulfilled the obligation after the fact, just as one fulfils it on Purim with nine verses. But if they read fewer than nine verses, they have not fulfilled the obligation (Shulḥan Arukh 137:4, and see Mishna Berura 137:14).

The Sages said (Megilla 21b) that even the verse "And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying" counts towards the number of verses. One might have thought that there must be new content in each of the three verses, and since this verse repeats itself many times in the Torah, it is not counted as one of the three verses. Therefore the Sages taught us that all the verses, without exception, are important and are counted in the number of verses. And the truth is that the verse "And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying" expresses the greatest novelty of all: that God Himself, in His glory, gave us the Torah through the greatest of the prophets, Moshe Rabbeinu.

sections.title_en: 7. The Reader and the One Called Up
sections.body_en:
At first the custom was that whoever was called up to the Torah would read by himself. And since the Torah scroll has no vowels and cantillation marks, every person would study the weekly portion well with the cantillation, in such a way that if he were called up to the Torah he could read his portion. And if he was called up to the Torah and had not yet managed to review the reading two or three times by himself, he would not go up (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 139:1). And so it is related of Rabbi Akiva that it once happened that he was called up to the Torah and did not want to go up. His disciples asked him: Did you not teach us, our master, that the Torah is our life and the length of our days? So why, when they called you up, did you not go up? He said to them: Because I had not arranged the reading by myself two or three times. For a person is not permitted to say a word of Torah before the public until he has gone over it by himself two or three times (Tanḥuma, Yitro 15). And so the Jews from Yemen are accustomed to this day, that each person called up reads his reading himself.

However, in the days of the Rishonim the custom spread in Sepharad and in Ashkenaz to appoint a 'ba'al korei' (reader) who reads for each person called up his portion, and the one called up recites the blessings before the reading and after it, and reads quietly with the reader word by word (see below halakha 11). There are two reasons for the custom: one, so as not to deprive those who do not know how to read properly, for without a 'ba'al korei' to read for them, they could not merit to go up to the Torah. And so that those who need someone to read for them will not be embarrassed, it became the custom that the 'ba'al korei' reads for all those called up (Rabbeinu Tam, Ran and Ritva). The second, there are people who tend to err in their reading but do not admit it, and if they are not allowed to read in the Torah – they will be insulted and quarrel. But when one of those who excel in reading is chosen as 'ba'al korei', they are not hurt (Rosh). According to both these reasons, even one who knows how to read should properly not read for himself in his aliya, but should fulfil his obligation through the reading of the 'ba'al korei'. And some of those of Sephardi origin are accustomed that if the person called up is known to be expert in the reading of all the portions, he reads for himself in his aliya.6

After the fact, when there is no one there who knows how to read with the cantillation, if there is among them a person who knows how to read with the cantillation but does not remember it, his friend may look in a Ḥumash and signal the cantillation to him or whisper it in his ear, and so he will read (Mishna Berura 142:8). And if this too is not possible, they should read without the cantillation, for reading with the cantillation is not indispensable, and they should even recite the blessings of the Torah over the reading (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 142:2).

notes_en.en:
The first reason was brought in the name of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot (Menaḥot 30a, s.v. 'Shmona'). Support for it comes from the Mishna in Bikkurim (3:7): "At first, whoever knew how to read – would read (the 'declaration of the first fruits' recited when bringing them to the kohen), and whoever did not know how to read – they would prompt him (so that he could bring the first fruits properly). People refrained from bringing (out of embarrassment at needing to be prompted), so they enacted that they would prompt both one who knows and one who does not know". And so wrote Tosafot (Megilla 21b, s.v. 'Tana'), Rabbeinu Baḥya (Devarim 26:1), the Ran (on the Rif) and the Ritva (on Megilla there). However, the Rosh (Megilla 3:1) raised a difficulty against their reason: for the first fruits they needed to enact prompting, because there is an obligation to bring first fruits, but there is no obligation for every individual to read in the Torah, and on the contrary, it is good that he be embarrassed that he did not learn, and as a result he will learn to read. Rather, since there were those who did not know how to read properly, and nevertheless went up and read incorrectly, and when they were corrected they were insulted, they instituted that there be a 'ba'al korei' who would read properly for all of them. And so wrote the Tur (Oraḥ Ḥayim 141).
According to these reasons, even a person called up who knows how to read – should not read by himself; and so wrote the Mishna Berura (141:8) and the Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 15. However, in the communities of those of Sephardi origin, some are accustomed that if the person called up is known to be expert in reading the Torah, they honour him to read his aliya (Rav Yosef Sharvit in Orḥot Yosher 1:7; Halakha Berura 141:5; and in the Responsa Divrei Malkiel 6:41 he encouraged those who are accustomed so to continue their custom).

sections.title_en: 8. Giving Precedence to the Kohen for the Sake of the Ways of Peace
sections.body_en:
Because of the great importance of being called up to the Torah, there is a concern that a quarrel will arise around the right to go up for the first aliyot. Therefore, among the enactments that the Sages enacted 'for the sake of the ways of peace' (Mishna Gittin 5:8-9), they enacted that the kohen be called up for the first aliya, and after him a levi and after him a yisrael. And although there is still great honour in the third aliya, which is the first of the aliyot fitting for a yisrael, since the first aliyot have already been allotted to the kohen and the levi, there is not so much concern that people will fight over it. In addition, some regard the sixth aliya as more important, and some were accustomed to honour the greatest of the public with the last aliya, which concludes the portion. And some regard the maftir aliya as more important, since the one called up for it recites many blessings. After all, one who quarrels over the honour of the aliyot harms the enactment of the Sages that was intended to preserve peace, and also disparages the other aliyot, as though they are not honourable.7

However, even without the enactment of the Sages, the kohen must be given precedence, for it is said concerning him "and you shall sanctify him" (Vayikra 21:8), to teach us that it is a mitzva to give him precedence in every holy matter. But in all other holy matters, if the kohen wishes to honour a yisrael who is greater than he in wisdom – he may do so. But in the Torah reading the kohen may not waive his honour and honour a yisrael who is greater than he in Torah; rather, the kohen always goes up first for the sake of the ways of peace (Gittin 59b; Shulḥan Arukh 135:4; Mishna Berura 9).

But if the kohen is an ignoramus (am ha-aretz) and the yisrael a Torah scholar, some say that the yisrael must be given precedence, as in the words of the Mishna (Horayot 13a), that even a yisrael who is a mamzer and a Torah scholar takes precedence over a High Priest who is an ignoramus. Not only that, but those who give precedence to an ignorant kohen transgress a prohibition, for they disgrace the honour of the Torah (Rashba 1:119). And some say that indeed this is the law with other honours, but concerning going up to the Torah, the kohen must be given precedence, for so the Sages enacted (Rav Amram Gaon and Rav Natronai Gaon). And so is the custom, to call up an ignorant kohen before a yisrael who is a Torah scholar (Shulḥan Arukh 135:4). However, if there is in the synagogue a kohen who is not an ignoramus, it is good to take care that he go up before a yisrael Torah scholar (Yam Shel Shlomo; Ḥayei Adam; and Biur Halakha 135:4).8

notes_en.en:
According to the words of the Sages, the third aliya is the most honourable for a yisrael, as they said (Gittin 60a; Shulḥan Arukh 136:1) that on Shabbatot and festivals, after the kohen and the levi, one should call up a Torah scholar who serves in a public position, and after him a Torah scholar fit for a public position, and after him ordinary Torah scholars. But since these are not the first aliyot, they were not concerned that people would quarrel over them. In addition, some wrote that people are not particular to call up for the aliyot of the yisrael according to the order of importance that the Sages stated (Levush 136:1; and see Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 136:2). And in Sepharad and in other places they were accustomed to regard the last aliya as important, and with it they honoured the great ones (Beit Yosef 135:4; Mishna Berura 136:5). And according to the Arizal, the most important aliya is the sixth, corresponding to the sefira of 'Yesod', and after it the third, corresponding to 'Tiferet'; and the virtue of the aliyot of the kohen and the levi is that in them one begins to reveal the lights that were hidden, and by virtue of this they are revealed afterwards more in the third and sixth aliyot (Sha'ar Ha-Kavanot, Derushei Keri'at Sefer Torah 2).
Beyond this, it is not fitting to quarrel over the aliyot, for by regarding one aliya as important, one diminishes the value of another, and the whole Torah is holy (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 136:2; Mishna Berura 282:18). And it is related even of the Levites that they would all run to carry the Ark and leave the table, and as a result they came to light-headedness and quarrelling and were punished (Bamidbar Rabba 5:1). And likewise they testified of the Rosh that when he saw that people did not want to go up for the fifth aliya – he went up regularly for this aliya (gloss to the Responsa Tashbetz 2:276).

When the yisrael is the greatest Torah scholar of the generation, it is permitted to give him precedence over the kohen even when the kohen is a Torah scholar. For they said (Gittin 59b) that they were accustomed to call up Rav Huna for the first aliya, because even "Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, the important kohanim of the Land of Israel, would bow to him" (for even the important kohanim of the Land of Israel were subordinate to him). And so wrote Tosafot, the Piskei Rid, the Ra'avya (Megilla 2:577), the Shibbolei Ha-Leket 32, the Darkhei Moshe (135:5) and others. And some say that it suffices that the Torah scholar be the greatest in the town (Rashba, Megilla 22a). However, in practice it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (135:4): "The plain custom is that even an ignorant kohen takes precedence to read before a great sage who is a yisrael, provided that the kohen knows how to read". The Derisha (135:1) and the Baḥ explained that in the last generations there is no Torah scholar to whom everyone is subordinate (similarly wrote the Tosafot Yom Tov, Gittin 5:8).

sections.title_en: 9. Customs of Those Called Up to the Torah
sections.body_en:
If they called up a kohen and there is no levi there, that same kohen is called up again for the second aliya in place of the levi. And he must bless again before the reading and after it, for the blessings are on the reading, and for every reading one must bless. And they should not call up another kohen, lest this arouse suspicion about the first kohen that he is blemished in lineage, and that this is why they called up a fit kohen in his place (Shulḥan Arukh 135:8).9

When there is no kohen there, even though there is a levi, yisraelim are called up for the first and second aliyot. And if they wish, they may call up a levi for the first aliya, but they should not call up a levi for the second aliya, so that people will not mistakenly think that the first was a kohen (Shulḥan Arukh 135:6; Mishna Berura 24).

A minyan made up entirely of kohanim calls up kohen after kohen, and if there is one yisrael or levi there, he goes up first for the sake of the ways of peace (Shulḥan Arukh 135:12; Mishna Berura 45). And if there is both one levi and one yisrael, first go up: kohen, levi and yisrael, according to the enactment of the Sages, and the rest are kohanim (Mishna Berura 43. And see Mishna Berura 44).

It is customary to honour with an aliya to the Torah a bridegroom during his seven days of feasting, and likewise the participants in a brit (the father of the boy, the mohel and the sandak) on the day of the brit mila. Many are accustomed to call up to the Torah on Shabbat also one who has in that week the anniversary (yahrzeit) of his father or mother (Sha'arei Efrayim 2:1).

On Shabbatot on which there is an important reading, such as the Ten Commandments and the Song of the Sea, it is customary to honour one of the dignitaries of the public with this aliya. And many were accustomed to honour the rabbi of the place with this aliya (Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 428:2; Le-David Emet 10:5).

In general, kohanim and leviyim are not called up for the other aliyot, lest suspicion arise about them that their lineage has been blemished. However, for maftir, since it is not among the seven people called up that the Sages enacted, a kohen or a levi is called up. And so that not a trace of suspicion will arise, the gabbai announces: "Let so-and-so the kohen stand up" or "the levi" (Rema 135:10; Mishna Berura 33).

Sometimes there is a need to call up more kohanim or leviyim, for example on a Shabbat Ḥatan or a bar mitzva of a family of kohanim or leviyim. When only one more aliya is needed, one may call up a kohen or a levi for the last aliya, and it is preferable that it be an additional aliya beyond the seven people called up. And the gabbai should say: "Let so-and-so stand up, even though he is a kohen" or "even though he is a levi". If there is a need for a further aliya, it is preferable that they repeat the order of 'kohen, levi and yisrael'. That is to say, for 'fourth' a kohen goes up, for 'fifth' a levi, and for 'sixth' a yisrael, and for the last a 'kohen'. And in case of need, they may call up kohen after kohen or levi after levi with a yisrael in between as a break, while saying 'even though he is a kohen' or 'levi'. That is to say, for 'fourth' a kohen goes up, for 'fifth' a yisrael, for 'sixth' a kohen, for 'seventh' a yisrael and for 'maftir' a kohen. And if they need to add another aliya for a kohen, they should add an eighth aliya for a kohen, and the 'maftir' too will be a kohen (based on weighing the views of the Shulḥan Arukh and the Rema 135:10, and the Mishna Berura 37; and see Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 7:5).

It is customary not to call up two brothers, or a father and son, one after the other (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 23:3, note 3).

One does not call up to the Torah a person who is engaged in another part of the prayer. And when he is the only kohen or levi: if he is in 'Pesukei De-Zimra' or in Taḥanun – he is called up, and if in the Shema and its blessings – he is not called up, and it is preferable that he leave the synagogue so that they will not mistakenly call him up.10

notes_en.en: It appears that when it happens many times that there is no levi, and it thus turns out that the same kohen goes up again and again for the first and second aliyot, it is right that most of the times the kohen leave when the first is called up (see Peri Ha-Sadeh 3:153). This is right both because of the derekh eretz of the kohen towards the rest of the worshippers, for it is not fitting that he take most of the aliyot, and because of the concern of an unnecessary blessing when he is called up in place of a levi, for according to the view of the author of the Ittur (Laws of the Mitzva of Hallel, siman 932, as brought in the Shibbolei Ha-Leket 34), the kohen does not bless in the second aliya, and some say that because of this he should say "Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le-olam va-ed" after his blessing on the second aliya (Mekor Barukh, Weisel 1; Yehuda Ya'aleh 1:45).

However, some hold that if he is the only kohen or levi, they should call him up even when he is in the Shema and its blessings (Nehar Shalom 135:1; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 66:9). However, according to most poskim one should not call him up. And it is right that he leave the synagogue so that they will not call him up (Olat Re'iya 1, p. 248). If they called up to the Torah a person who is in the Shema and its blessings: according to the custom of those of Sephardi origin he should not go up (Rashba 1:185; Shulḥan Arukh 66:4; Peri Ḥadash; Ḥida in Kesher Gudal 11:23; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 24), and according to the custom of those of Ashkenazi origin he should go up (Manhig; Levush; Leḥem Ḥamudot, Berakhot 2:23; Magen Avraham 8; Mishna Berura 66:26). But if they mistakenly called up a person who is in the middle of 'Pesukei De-Zimra', according to all views he should go up because of the honour of the public (Mishna Berura 51:10; Peninei Halakha, Prayer 14:4). If there is no one who knows how to read in the Torah except the one who is in the Shema and its blessings, he may interrupt and read in the Torah, because of the honour of the Torah (Mishna Berura 66:26). If they called up a person while he is in the middle of the Amida prayer – he should not go up (Rema 104:7).

sections.title_en: 10. Giving Precedence to the Kohen on Weekdays
sections.body_en:
The enactment to give precedence to a kohen was on Shabbatot and festivals, on which many gathered in the synagogue; but on Mondays and Thursdays, on which the worshippers were few, since there was no concern of dispute, it was permitted to call up a yisrael for the first aliya (Gittin 59b). However, several Rishonim wrote that this was so in the time of the Mishna and the Gemara, when people were busy with their work and only a few came to pray with a minyan on weekdays. But in the days of the Rishonim, when more people came to the prayer on weekdays, on weekdays too the kohen must be given precedence (Tosafot there, s.v. 'Aval'; Semag and Mordekhai). On the other hand, some Rishonim hold that there is no need to give precedence to the kohen on weekdays, for although the worshippers with a minyan have increased, they are still not as many as on Shabbatot and festivals (Rosh, Rid and Ra'avya). In practice, the Aḥaronim wrote that on weekdays too one must take care to give precedence to the kohen (Shulḥan Arukh 135:3; Mishna Berura 9).11

Sometimes on Mondays and Thursdays there are in the synagogue two yisraelim who need to be called up, such as a bridegroom and a participant in a brit, and if they call up a kohen and a levi for the first aliyot, two aliyot will not remain for them. Therefore, they ask the kohen to leave when the first is called up, and in this way they can call up the bridegroom and the participant in the brit. And even if the kohen does not wish to leave, one may call up the bridegroom or the participant in the brit for the first aliya, because in case of need one may rely on those who hold that on weekdays there is no need to give precedence to the kohen.12

notes_en.en: Some Rishonim hold that on weekdays too one must take care to call up a kohen first, since in their days more people were accustomed to come to the prayer on weekdays (Tosafot, Gittin 59b, s.v. 'Aval'; Semag, positive commandments 171; Semak of Zurich 56; Mordekhai 401; Or Zarua 2:42; and they wrote that this is the view of Rabbeinu Tam. And so it is implied by the Rif and the Rambam, who wrote without qualification that a kohen always reads first). On the other hand, some hold that on weekdays, since the public is small, there is no enactment for the sake of the ways of peace, and the kohen may waive 'and you shall sanctify him' so that a yisrael may go up first (Rosh, Gittin 5:20; Tur 135; Piskei Rid, Ritva and Nimukei Yosef on Gittin 59b; Ra'avya part 2, Megilla 577; and Rivash 204). In practice, almost all the Aḥaronim wrote that on weekdays too one must take care to call up a kohen first, among them: the Beit Yosef (135:5) and the Peri Megadim (Mishbetzot Zahav 135:3). And the Ḥayei Adam (31:17) and the Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 13 wrote that even in a small minyan one must give precedence to the kohen.

Some say that even on Shabbat and on a festival, on a one-time basis and in case of need, the kohen may waive his honour so that a yisrael may go up in his place, for example when they wish to receive a large donation for the first aliya, or because many guests need to be honoured (Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 25; Rashk, Sefer STaM, Peret Ve-Olelot 86:1). On the other hand, some hold that the kohen should not give up his aliya on Shabbat and on a festival (Knesset Yeḥezkel 7; Rav Gutmacher, Aderet Eliyahu, Oraḥ Ḥayim 16).
On weekdays: some say that when two bridegrooms who are yisraelim need to be honoured, one may add another aliya (Mordekhai, Megilla 808 in the name of the Riva; Hagahot Maimoniyot; Rema 135:1; Erekh Leḥem 135:1; Birkei Yosef 4; Shemesh U-Magen 1:17). And one need not be concerned about loss of working time and the burden on the public, since by virtue of the bridegrooms Taḥanun is not said, and then time remains to add an aliya (Birkei Yosef 135:5). And also because the public waives its honour for the sake of the bridegrooms (Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Ha-Tur 282:11). However, according to most poskim one should not add people called up, according to the plain meaning of the Mishna in Megilla 21a (Beit Yosef in Bedek Ha-Bayit 135:1; Magen Avraham 2; Taz 2; Eliya Rabba 1; Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 135:1; Ma'amar Mordekhai 135:1; Mishna Berura 135:3; Yabi'a Omer 6:23; Aseh Lekha Rav 3:22).
Therefore, the solution is that the kohen give up his aliya, and it is preferable that he leave the synagogue at the moment when the first aliya is called, and immediately after the one called up begins to bless – he should come back in. And indeed some say that without his leaving it is forbidden to call up a yisrael (Magen Avraham 135:7, based on the Maharik), but in halakha one may call up a yisrael with his consent even if he does not leave (Beit Yosef and Rema 135:5; Mishna Berura 18; Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:34; Yabi'a Omer 6:23; Si'aḥ Naḥum 7). And it appears that in case of need, even if the kohen does not agree to give up his aliya, one may call up the bridegrooms, for we have learned that according to many Rishonim on weekdays there is no obligation to give precedence to a kohen, and in a pressing situation one may rely on them.

sections.title_en: 11. May One Call Up Someone Who Cannot Read, or a Blind Person?
sections.body_en:
The person called up must read quietly with the ba'al korei word by word, for at first the person called up would read aloud for everyone; therefore, even though the custom now is that the 'ba'al korei' reads for everyone, at the very least the person called up must read along with him quietly. But he should take care that his voice not be heard by those standing beside him or by the 'ba'al korei', so as not to disturb them.

Some say that one should not call up to the Torah someone who does not know how to read, or a blind person who is unable to read, because the mitzva is that the person called up read quietly in the Torah, and it is on this that he blesses. But if he knows a little how to read, and together with the reader he is able to follow the reading and say it quietly, he may be called up (Shulḥan Arukh 139:2).

And some say that one may call up to the Torah even someone who does not know how to read, or a blind person, for after the fact, by hearing the reading of the ḥazan he fulfils his obligation, for the law of one who hears is like that of one who utters the words with his mouth, and over this he recites the blessings of the Torah (Rema). And so is the prevalent custom in most communities of Israel, and only a community in which it is known that the custom was not to call up someone who is unable to read may continue in its custom13

notes_en.en:
Some say that the person called up must read quietly in a way that he does not let his own ear hear it (Shulḥan Arukh 141:2), for so they said in the Zohar (Vayakhel 206a). And some are not concerned for the words of the Zohar, and hold that he may let his own ear hear it (Rema there), provided that he does not disturb those standing beside him from hearing or the ba'al korei from reading.
The Rosh wrote (Responsa, rule 3:12) that one should not call up to the Torah someone who cannot read, because the person called up must read by himself, and if not – his blessings are in vain. And the Maharam of Rothenburg wrote (149) that he must do so by reading from the text, for if he repeats by heart after the ba'al korei, he will transgress the prohibition of saying by heart things that are written. And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (141:2-3), the Knesset Ha-Gedola (Hagahot Beit Yosef 141), the She'ilat Yavetz (1:75) and others. However, many hold that it is permitted to call up someone who does not know how to read, or a blind person, because after the fact the person called up can fulfil his obligation through what he hears from the reader (Taz 141:3; Mishna Berura 12-13). And so wrote the Agudda (Bava Kamma chapter 8, 104), the Nimukei Yosef (Megilla 24a) in the name of the Eshkol, and the Maharil (Laws of the Torah Reading 3). And so ruled the Rema (139:3), the Magen Avraham 4, the Ḥayei Adam (31:37), the Nehar Mitzrayim (Laws of the Torah Reading 13), the Mayim Ḥayim (Mashash, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:257) and the Aseh Lekha Rav (6:20), and the She'al Ha-Ish (Oraḥ Ḥayim 2) inclined to this. And some say that it is right, when possible, that he read by heart after the ba'al korei. And there is no need to be concerned that he will be saying written things by heart, for only when he thereby fulfils the obligation of the public is there a prohibition in this (Binyamin Ze'ev 245, and Mas'at Binyamin 62; see above 8:7). In addition, the care not to say written things by heart is for the choicest fulfilment of the mitzva, but for a great need it is permitted (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 139:8), or they permitted it because 'it is a time to act for the Lord' (Mekor Ḥayim of the Ḥavot Ya'ir 139:2-3).

sections.title_en: 12. The Prohibition of Speaking During the Torah Reading
sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Sota 39a) that because of the honour of the Torah, from the time the Torah scroll is opened in order to read from it, it is forbidden for the congregation to speak with one another, even about a matter of halakha. And so it is said (Neḥemya 8:5): "And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and when he opened it – all the people stood up". 'Stood' (amdu) means they stopped all speech and fell silent. And so it is said (there 8:3): "And he read in it… from the light until midday, before the men and the women and those who could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive to the book of the Torah". The Sages further said (Zohar part 2, 206a) that everyone must prepare themselves for the Torah reading with awe and fear, with trembling and quaking, and direct their hearts to the Torah as though they were standing now at Mount Sinai to receive the Torah.

And so many ruled in halakha, that during the reading all those present in the synagogue must listen to the Torah reading, and even between one person called up and the next it is forbidden to speak words of Torah (Rif, Rambam and Rashba).

On the other hand, some hold that the prohibition is to speak with another, but a person is permitted to study Torah quietly during the Torah reading, on condition that there are ten who are listening to the reading (Behag, Tosafot and Rosh). The poskim disagreed in explaining their view: some say that since there is no personal obligation on the individual to hear the Torah reading (above halakha 1), one who wishes may study Torah quietly on another subject instead of listening to the reading, on condition that there are ten who will listen to the reading (so it is implied by the Shulḥan Arukh 146:2; Tzitz Eliezer 18:5). And some say that all those present in the synagogue are obligated to listen to the Torah reading, since they are part of the public that is obligated in its reading, and only one who has already heard the Torah reading in an earlier minyan may study quietly while the Torah is being read (Biur Halakha 146:2, s.v. 'Ve-yesh').

In practice, it is right to be stringent not to study anything during the reading but to listen to the ba'al korei, for so many poskim ruled, and even those who are lenient agree that it is right to conduct oneself so ideally.

Also in the pause between the aliyot it is forbidden to study Torah aloud, and all the more so it is forbidden to speak with one's friend about words of Torah, but it is permitted to study quietly (Rabbeinu Yona; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 146:2; Eliya Rabba 4). And some are lenient to converse quietly about words of Torah, especially when the gabbaim lengthen the saying of 'Mi She-berakh', on condition that the conversation is about words of Torah and does not continue also during the blessings and the reading (Baḥ; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 146:3).14

Although according to many it is forbidden to speak in the pauses between the aliyot even about words of Torah, the rabbi is permitted to answer an urgent question in the pauses between the aliyot (Mishna Berura 146:6). The gabbaim too are permitted to speak in the pauses about necessary matters connected with the prayer. And when the question is very urgent, the rabbi is permitted to answer even during the reading (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 146:2). And likewise the gabbai is permitted to speak about urgent matters that cannot be postponed, such as clarifying whom to honour with an aliya to the Torah in order to prevent an insult or a burden on the public.

notes_en.en:
Sota (39a): "Rava bar Rav Huna said: Once the Torah scroll has been opened – it is forbidden to talk, even about a matter of halakha". However, there is a difficulty, for we learned in Berakhot (8a): "Rav Sheshet would turn his face away and study (he turned his face and studied), saying: We are occupied with ours and they with theirs" (I am occupied with mine and they are occupied with theirs). The Rishonim disagreed in explaining the practice of Rav Sheshet. Some are stringent and hold that only for one whose Torah is his profession, like Rav Sheshet, is it permitted to engage in Torah during the reading, but for everyone else it is forbidden, as explained in Sota (39a). This is the view of the Rif, the Rambam (Prayer 12:9) and the Rashba (1:206). And so is the view of Rabbeinu Ḥananel (as brought in the Or Zarua).
On the other hand, some are lenient and hold that the prohibition is to study aloud, because of the affront to the honour of the Torah reading, but to study quietly is permitted, as Rav Sheshet did. This is the view of Tosafot (Berakhot 8a) and the Rosh (there 1:7). And the Behag wrote (siman 24) that the permission is on condition that there are ten there who are listening to the reading. And it appears that Tosafot and the Rosh agree to this (Terumat Ha-Deshen 24; Mishna Berura 146:8). And Rabbeinu Yona (Berakhot 4a) wrote that the permission to study during the Torah reading is conditional on his beginning to study before the start of the reading, so that he will be considered one who is engaged in a mitzva and exempt from the mitzva of hearing the Torah reading. And some say that even according to those who are stringent (Rabbeinu Ḥananel and the Rif), it is permitted to study during the reading shenayim mikra ve-eḥad targum, and so Rabbi Yehuda He-Ḥasid would do (Or Zarua 1, Laws of the Shema 11; Mordekhai, Hagahot Asheri and Semak).
In practice, the Beit Yosef wrote (146:2) that since great and many authorities were lenient, those who wish to study during the reading have something to rely on. And in the Shulḥan Arukh there he wrote that shenayim mikra ve-eḥad targum is permitted, and this is implied even according to those who are stringent. Simply, it is implied that the intention of the lenient authorities and the Shulḥan Arukh is that even one who has not heard the reading himself may study quietly during the public reading, for a person has no personal obligation to hear the Torah reading. And so wrote the Tzitz Eliezer (18:5). However, some hold that all the words of the lenient authorities apply only to one who has already heard the Torah reading, but if he has not heard it, since he is with the public, he is obligated to hear it (Biur Halakha 146:2, s.v. 'Ve-yesh'). And this is the proper guidance, for according to those who are stringent, and even according to the lenient ones as understood by the Biur Halakha, one who has not heard the Torah reading is obligated to hear the ba'al korei. And even according to the lenient ones, the Shulḥan Arukh wrote that it is right for one who is meticulous to listen to the Torah reading.

sections.title_en: 13. The Honour of the Torah and of the Public When Taking Out the Scroll and During the Reading
sections.body_en:
Rolling a Torah scroll from its beginning to its end takes several minutes. So as not to waste the time of the public, who would be idle while the Torah scroll is rolled to the place where it must be read on Shabbat or a festival, the gabbaim must roll the Torah scroll before the prayer, so that they can read from it immediately. However, when the public has only one Torah scroll, and two readings must be read in the Torah, they wait in order to roll the scroll for the second reading, for the public waives its honour in order to fulfil the reading in the two places according to the enactment of the Sages (Yoma 70a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 144:3; Magen Avraham 7).

If by mistake they took out another Torah scroll that is not rolled to the place of the reading, some say that one does not return it to the ark, so as not to harm its honour and arouse suspicion about it that it is defective. And although the public will have to wait until it is rolled to the place of the reading, the honour of the Torah scroll prevails (Shemesh Tzedaka, Oraḥ Ḥayim 31; Mateh Yehuda, Ayash, Oraḥ Ḥayim 282:15; Erekh Ha-Shulḥan 144:5). And some say that it is permitted to return it to the ark and take out the scroll that is properly rolled, because of the burden on the public, and so that people will not think that the scroll is defective, the gabbai should announce why they returned it (Yafeh La-Lev part 5, 144:1; Eshel Avraham of Butshash 144:1). In practice, if the ḥazan is still standing near the Holy Ark, it is preferable to return it so as not to burden the public. And if the scroll has already reached the bima, many are accustomed to roll the scroll, and those who wish to rely on the view of those concerned about the burden on the public and to exchange it – may do so.

It is customary that the one carrying the Torah scroll from the ark to the bima and back walks on the right side and holds the scroll on his right side (Rema 134:2; Mishna Berura 141:25). The whole public is obligated to stand while the scroll is carried, and many are accustomed to say verses in praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, and of the Torah, and some add prayers and requests. Many are accustomed to kiss the Torah scroll with their mouths or to touch it with the hand or with the tzitzit and kiss them. One who is ill or has a cold must take care not to kiss the Torah with his mouth, so that he does not infect others with his illness.

Because of the honour of the Torah, it is forbidden to leave the synagogue from the time the Torah reading begins until its end. The Sages said (Berakhot 8a) that of one who leaves in the middle of the Torah reading it is said (Yeshayahu 1:28): "And they that forsake the Lord shall be consumed". And one who needs to leave, for example one who needs the toilet, may leave between the reading of one person called up and the next, for then the Torah scroll is closed, and the affront to the honour of the Torah is less (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 146:1). But to leave without need is forbidden even between the aliyot.15

As we learned (above 9:6), because of the holiness of the Torah scroll, when it must be rolled, one must take care not to touch the parchment with bare hands; rather, the scroll is rolled with the help of the 'atzei ḥayim' on which the scroll is rolled, or it is rolled with the help of a cloth.

There is no obligation to stand during the Torah reading. However, some are particular to stand, just as at the Revelation at Mount Sinai everyone stood (Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 146:4). And some say that one must stand when responding to 'Barekhu', because it is a devar she-bi-kedusha, and one must stand while a devar she-bi-kedusha is said (Mishna Berura 146:18). However, according to many, there is no need to stand at all during the Torah reading (Shulḥan Arukh 146:4). And so the holy Arizal would sit throughout the reading and during the saying of 'Barekhu' (Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 146:20). And so many of those of Sephardi and Ashkenazi origin are accustomed. However, when responding to 'Barekhu', which is a short response, many of those of Ashkenazi origin are accustomed to rise slightly from the chair. And at the reading of the Ten Commandments many from all the communities are accustomed to stand (Peninei Halakha, Mo'adim 13:11, note 4).

notes_en.en: Berakhot (8a): "Rabbi Abahu would go out between one man and the next". And so wrote most of the Rishonim and the Shulḥan Arukh (146:1): "It is forbidden to go out and leave the Torah scroll while it is open, but between one man and the next it is permitted". The Erekh Ha-Shulḥan (146:2) learned from this that it is permitted to leave between the aliyot even without need. And so wrote the Halikhot Olam (part 3, Toledot 17, p. 134), and that this is the view of the Shulḥan Arukh, because the Torah reading is an enactment of the public and not of the individual. On the other hand, the Agudda (Berakhot 8a), the Mahari Abuhav (Oraḥ Ḥayim 146) and the Seder Ha-Yom (Laws of the Torah Reading on Shabbat) wrote that the permission to leave between the aliyot is only for a great need. And so wrote many Aḥaronim in practice (Magen Avraham 146:2; Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Ha-Tur 146:1; Eliya Rabba 2; Mishna Berura 3; Ḥayei Adam 31:2; Ben Ish Ḥai, Toledot, second year 20). Apparently they understood that the Rishonim did not need to explain that the permission is only for a great need because this is obvious. Above I wrote in the middle way, that the permission to leave is for a 'need'.

sections.title_en: 14. Hagbaha
sections.body_en:
Because of the honour of the Torah, the Torah scroll is lifted so that the whole public will see the place where the reading is, "for it is a mitzva for all the men and women to see the writing, and to bow slightly and say (Devarim 4:44): And this is the Torah which Moshe set before the children of Israel" (Tractate Soferim 14:8). According to the custom of those of Sephardi origin and some of those of Ashkenazi origin, the scroll is lifted before the reading (Shulḥan Arukh 134:2; the Arizal), and according to the custom of most of those of Ashkenazi origin it is lifted after the reading (Rema there). The scroll must be open at the place of the reading during the lifting, and if it was open at another place – there is no need to go back and lift it again.

The one lifting must take care that all the worshippers can see the letters of the Torah. For this purpose it is good that he make a full turn slowly, and in this way everyone will see the letters. In a Torah scroll made according to the custom of those of Ashkenazi origin, the one lifting opens the scroll so that three columns of it will be seen (Mishna Berura 134:8). Those of Sephardi origin are accustomed that while the scroll is being lifted one of the worshippers points to the place of the reading. Those of Yemenite origin were accustomed not to lift the Torah scroll for fear that it would fall; rather, while the scroll lies on the bima, the one lifting takes hold of the sheet itself by means of a cloth and raises it from side to side in such a way that three columns are seen (Maharitz, Etz Ḥayim 63:1).

As stated, it is a mitzva for all the men and women who see the writing to bow slightly (Tractate Soferim 14:8; Shulḥan Arukh 134:2). Many of those of Ashkenazi origin were not accustomed to bow, and some found a justification for this, but ideally it is fitting to bow when one sees the writing (Har Tzvi, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:64). In the last generations a custom has spread that expresses affection for the Torah, according to which, during the lifting, people point at the Torah scroll with a finger or with the tzitzit, and afterwards kiss it.

The Sages said (Megilla 32a) that the one who rolls, meaning the one who lifts, receives a reward equal to all those who went up to the Torah, because he is engaged in the honour of the Torah. Therefore it is fitting to honour one of the dignitaries of the congregation with the lifting, provided that he has the strength to lift the scroll without concern that it will fall from his hands. And it is possible that for this reason many were accustomed to honour young men with the lifting, as there is no concern that they will fail in lifting the scroll (Shulḥan Arukh 147:1; Mishna Berura 7; 19).

After the one rolling has finished rolling the scroll and closing it, the maftir may begin the blessing of the haftara, and need not wait until the one rolling binds it and covers it with the mantle (Sha'arei Efrayim 10:18; Peri Megadim 147:10). And some are accustomed to wait until he finishes covering it with the mantle (see Mishna Berura 147:22).

sections.title_en: 15. Calling Up a Minor
sections.body_en:
The Sages said in the Mishna (Megilla 24a): "A minor reads in the Torah and translates". Seemingly there is a difficulty: how can a minor fulfil the obligation of the public, when in all other holy matters a minor cannot fulfil the obligation of an adult?

Some say that the Sages ruled so because of necessity: since each person called up would read his own aliya, and sometimes there were not found in the minyan seven men who knew how to read in the Torah, they were lenient in case of need to call up to the Torah also minors who had learned to read properly (Rivash). According to their view, since it became the custom that one person reads the whole portion for the seven people called up, there is no longer a need to be lenient in this, and therefore one should not call up a minor among the seven. And so many were accustomed. But for maftir, which is not among the seven – some are accustomed to call up a minor; and those of Ashkenazi origin and some of those of Sephardi origin are accustomed not to call up a minor even for maftir.

And some say that by the essence of the enactment there is no need for the person called up to the Torah to fulfil the obligation of the public through his reading; rather, the main thing is that the public hear the Torah reading, and therefore it is permitted to call up a minor to the Torah even ideally. However, even according to this view, in the opinion of many, only when seven people are called up may minors be called up for some of the aliyot. And so those of Yemenite origin and some of those of Sephardi origin are accustomed.16

notes_en.en:
Many wrote that a minor may go up to the Torah like an adult. So wrote, in the name of R. Simḥa: the Maharam of Rothenburg (108), the Hagahot Maimoniyot (Prayer 12:70) and the Mordekhai (Gittin 386). And so wrote the Rambam (Prayer 12:17), the Or Zarua (1:752), the Me'iri (Megilla 23a) and the Tashbetz (Ḥut Ha-Meshulash 3:31).
However, some explained that the ruling to call up a minor is for a pressing situation or because of need, when there are not enough adults to read in the Torah. So it is written in the Responsa of the Rambam (184) concerning a reading of three. And so wrote the Rivash (326): "When they enacted that seven should read in the Torah, the enactment was that a minor who knows how to read would go up among the seven, so as not to burden the public that all seven be adults, for perhaps they would not find ones who know how to read". And the Tzitz Eliezer brought this (7:1, Kuntres Katan Le-Maftir 5:15). Consequently, when there is a ba'al korei who knows the reading well, there is no longer a need to call up minors. And so wrote R. Yosef Ya'ish (Ben Avraham, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1), that a minor is not called up among the three or the seven, "for there are many adults in the synagogue, and one should not leave the adults and call up the minors". And so wrote the Kaf Ha-Ḥayim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 135:18).
In practice, some say that even today, when one person reads for everyone, it is possible to call up a minor like an adult. So wrote the Erekh Ha-Shulḥan (Oraḥ Ḥayim 135:1), the Responsa Gur Aryeh Yehuda (Oraḥ Ḥayim 30) and the Mayim Ḥayim (Mashash 2:86). And so wrote the Va-Yomer Yitzḥak (Likkutei Dinim, Laws of a Torah Scroll 17) and the Yeḥaveh Da'at (2:15), concerning a minor who has already begun to put on tefillin. And according to many, a minor may be called up only among the seven, but not among the three. So wrote the Rambam (in his Commentary on the Mishna, Megilla 4:6, in the name of a Gaon), the Roke'aḥ (56), the Knesset Ha-Gedola (282:12), the Olat Shabbat (282:3), the Ḥasdei David (Megilla 3:5), the Nehar Mitzrayim (Nefilat Apayim 3), the Be'er Mayim (10), the Petaḥ Ha-Devir (3, 282:6-7), the Mikveh Ha-Mayim (3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 26), the Yalkut Shemesh (110) and the Yeḥaveh Da'at (4:23). And some say that a minor goes up only for the seventh aliya (Tosafot, Rosh Ha-Shana 33a; Hagahot Maimoniyot, Prayer 12:60. And so wrote the Ginat Veradim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:22; and the Ben Ish Ḥai, second year, Toledot 17, according to the Kabbala). According to the custom of Yemen, a minor is called up among the seven and for maftir, but when a second scroll is taken out for maftir, many were accustomed not to call up a minor (Va-Yitzbor Yosef Bar 2:15).
On the other hand, already some three hundred years ago some were accustomed that a minor does not go up to the Torah at all (Mateh Yehuda 282:6; Ma'aseh Roke'aḥ, Prayer 12:17. And see Tashbetz 2:261). However, for maftir many were lenient to call up a minor (Beit Yosef in the name of the Roke'aḥ; Perisha 282:5; Magen Avraham 6; Mishna Berura 12; Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh of Rav Refael Barukh Toledano 1:122:10; Yaskil Avdi 7, Oraḥ Ḥayim 6), and so is the custom of Tunis (Alei Hadas 6:37) and Libya (Higgid Mordekhai, siman 70). And the custom of those of Ashkenazi origin is that a minor is not called up even for maftir. And so is the custom of Algeria (Mateh Yehuda, cited above). If a boy came for a bar mitzva reading in the synagogue, and it became clear to the gabbaim that a mistake occurred and he is not yet thirteen years old, since this is a pressing situation they may call him up to the Torah.
Women: A baraita in Megilla (23a): "All may go up among the seven, even a minor and even a woman. But the Sages said: A woman should not read in the Torah, because of the honour of the public". Most of the Rishonim copied the baraita as it is worded, and the Rambam (Prayer 12:17) omitted the first part and wrote: "A woman should not read in public, because of the honour of the public". Some explained that the honour of the public is harmed when there is no one among them who knows how to read and they are forced to fulfil their obligation through the reading of a woman. Similar to what the Sages said, that a curse will come upon a man whose wife and children bless for him (Rabbi Avraham Min Ha-Har, Megilla 19b). And one explained that there is a lack of modesty in women being called up (Mayim Ḥayim, Mashash 2:140). Rabbeinu Manoaḥ wrote that were it not for the reason of the honour of the public, women could go up to the Torah, "just as the Torah was given to Israel the males, it was given also to the females", and although they were not commanded in Torah study like males, "nevertheless they were commanded in the mitzvot written in the Torah, and if so they can bless 'asher baḥar banu' and 'asher natan lanu' and read in the Torah like men, were it not for the honour of the public". And there were poskim who wrote that in a small home minyan women go up to the Torah. So wrote the Sefer Ha-Battim (Laws of the Torah Reading 2), "for it is called a public only when they pray in the synagogue". And so wrote the Yavetz (Migdal Oz, Shoket 2:10). And the Maharam of Rothenburg (Responsa, Lvov edition 402) wrote that in a town where there are only kohanim, from the third aliya onwards women should go up to the Torah, for if kohanim go up people will suspect that they are ḥalalim, sons of divorcees, and it is preferable that "the honour of the public be set aside because of a blemish on the kohanim". And Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 2:3) and the Mordekhai (Gittin 404) brought him. However, the rest of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not mention a situation in which women are called up to the Torah, and so is the custom from generations past, that women do not go up to the Torah.

sections.title_en: 16. Which Error Invalidates the Reading
sections.body_en:
The ba'al korei must prepare the reading well, so that he can read precisely and fluently, for the honour of the Torah and the honour of the public. If the reader erred in his reading in the vowels of the letters, some say that even when the error did not cause a change in the meaning of the word, he is corrected so that he will go back and read precisely (Rambam; Shulḥan Arukh 142:1). On the other hand, some say that so as not to embarrass him, even when the error caused a change of meaning, or he added or omitted a letter, he is not corrected (Ha-Manhig; Baḥ). And according to the middle view, an error that changes the meaning is corrected, and an error that does not change it is not corrected (Rema).

In practice, in a place where they were accustomed according to the view of the stringent to point out every error, as long as no great insult or quarrels result from it, it is right that they continue in their custom. However, in a place where there is no custom – it is right to follow the middle view, that an error that changes the meaning of the word – is corrected, and an error that does not change it – is not corrected. For example, if he read yashav instead of yoshev, since he changed between the meaning of past and present, he is made to go back. And likewise if he read ya'aseh instead of ye'aseh, since he changed between the meaning of active and passive, he is made to go back. Also if he erred in the cantillation with an error that causes a change in the understanding of the sentence, he is made to go back (Mishna Berura 142:4). But an error that does not change the meaning should not be pointed out and corrected, for example if he read yada'tem with the stress on the penultimate syllable instead of on the last. And even when grammatically there is a change of meaning, if only the grammarians notice it, one should not make him go back for it. As today most readers are not particular about distinguishing between a word with a dagesh and a word without a dagesh. For example, in the verse (Bereshit 1:10): "and the gathering together of the waters He called seas (yammim)", people mistakenly read 'yamim' without a dagesh in the 'mem', even though the grammatical meaning of this word is 'day' in the plural and not 'sea' in the plural.

If he omitted or added a letter in a way that does not change the meaning, for example he read Mitzriyim with two yods instead of Mitzrayim with one yod, ideally they should correct him according to the view of the stringent, but if he continued with the reading, or there is a concern of insult, there is no need to correct him (Eliya Rabba; Mishna Berura 142:4).

When there is a concern of a great insult, even if the reader made an error that changes the meaning, since the law is rabbinic, one should rely on the view of the lenient and refrain from pointing it out to him, so as not to embarrass him. In addition, in such a case there is a concern that the reader will become anxious, which will cause him to err more, and so his insult will grow and the honour of the reading will be harmed more. The proper advice for a place where there is a concern that those correcting will hurt the reader is that they station beside the ba'al korei a person who is expert in grammar, and only he will have permission to correct the reader. And in a place where there is a concern of a great insult, such as with a 'bar mitzva' boy, he should follow the view of the lenient and not correct. But he should make sure that in future they do not appoint a reader who is liable to make many errors, and likewise he should test the bar mitzva boys, and guide one for whom the reading is difficult – to make do with reading the maftir.17

notes_en.en:
Three views on the law of an error: a) For every error he is made to go back, as we learned in the Yerushalmi Megilla (4:5): "Even if he erred between 'im' and 've-im' – he is made to go back". And so wrote the Rambam (Prayer 12:6), that if "he read and erred, even in the precision of a single letter – he is made to go back, until he reads it precisely". And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 142:1). b) Even when they erred and changed the meaning of the word – they have fulfilled the obligation, and therefore there is no need to make the reader go back for his error, as they said in Shir Ha-Shirim Rabba (2:4, according to the version of the Rishonim): "From where do we know that if he read 'Aharon' as 'Haron', he has fulfilled his obligation? For it is said: and his banner over me was love", and Tosafot brought it (Avoda Zara 22b, s.v. 'Regla'), the Hagahot Asheri in the name of the Ri (Shabbat 6:13:2), and others. On this basis the Manhig wrote (Shabbat 31) that one who errs in the Torah reading should not be made to go back, so as not to embarrass him in public. Similarly the Terumat Ha-Deshen wrote (Pesakim U-Khetavim 181) that he saw his teachers "and other great ones" that when the reader erred "they rebuked him a little; nevertheless none of them made him go back". That is to say, they pointed it out to him so that he would correct it immediately, but if he did not correct it immediately they did not ask him to go back, because the error does not invalidate. Similarly the Maharil wrote (Ha-Ḥadashot 23) that in a pressing situation, when there is no one who can read without errors, a reader who errs may read. And so wrote the Mahari ben Ḥaviv in his first distinction, as brought in the Beit Yosef (142:1). And the Baḥ (Oraḥ Ḥayim 142:1) ruled like the 'Manhig'. And the Eliya Rabba (2) wrote that one should not protest against one who conducts himself so. And in the 'Torat Ḥayim' (1) he wrote that one may rely on the Manhig in a pressing situation. And Rav Gaguine wrote (Keter Shem Tov 1, p. 286) that so was the custom of the Sephardim in London and Amsterdam.
c) The middle view: for an error that changes the meaning he is made to go back, and for an error that does not change it he is not made to go back. So wrote the Mahari ben Ḥaviv in his second distinction, brought in the Beit Yosef (142:1). And so wrote most poskim, among them: the Rema (142:1), the Magen Avraham 1, the Peri Megadim (Eshel Avraham 1), the Eshel Avraham of Butshash (1), the Mishna Berura 4 and the Mishpetei Uziel (part 3, Addenda to Oraḥ Ḥayim 142:8). The Rema added, based on the Terumat Ha-Deshen, that in any event one should rebuke one who makes errors, so that in future he will prepare his reading better. And so wrote the Responsa Beit Ya'akov 76, the Mekor Ḥayim (in Bakharakh 142:1) and the Ravid Ha-Zahav 41. And the Eshel Avraham of Butshash explained (Tinyana 142, s.v.
