'Ma she-katuv') that the intention is that they rebuke the reader discreetly after the reading. And the Sha'arei Raḥamim brought it (on the Sha'arei Efrayim 3:20). And the Eshel Avraham of Butshash added (Kama 142:1) that when the ba'al korei was not negligent in preparing the reading, he would not rebuke him.
Concerning the omission or addition of a letter that does not change the meaning, some say that he must go back, according to the first view, and perhaps also according to the third view, for perhaps in their view he is not made to go back only for a change of meaning without the omission or addition of a letter, but when there is an omission or addition of a letter he is made to go back. And so wrote the Peri Ḥadash (142:1), the Ravid Ha-Zahav (41), the Biur Ha-Gra (1), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (1-4) and the Kaf Ha-Ḥayim (2). And some say that he is not made to go back, so according to the second view, as the 'Manhig' wrote based on Shir Ha-Shirim Rabba. And some say that even according to the third view he is not made to go back, since there is no change of meaning (Eliya Rabba 142:2; Mishna Berura 4).
An example of an error in the cantillation that changes the meaning of the verse (Shemot 17:9): "And Moshe said to Yehoshua: Choose us men, and go out, fight with Amalek; tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand". The 'etnaḥta' should be under the word 'Amalek', and then the meaning is that tomorrow Moshe will stand on the top of the hill. And if he changed it and placed the 'etnaḥta' under the word 'tomorrow', an error results according to which the meaning of the verse is that the war will be tomorrow (see Yoma 52b).

sections.title_en: 17. How to Correct When They Continued Reading After the Error
sections.body_en:
If the reader made an error that changes the meaning, even if they noticed the error only after he continued reading, he must go back and read the word properly, and continue reading from it onwards in order, until the end of the reading of that aliya. When going back to that word is not intelligible, because it is in the middle of a passage, one must go back to the beginning of the verse in which the error was made. But if the reader corrected himself immediately, even if the word was in the middle of a sentence, there is no need to go back to its beginning.

When an error was made in the reading of the first person called up, and only after several aliyot did they conclude that an error had been made: since there is great trouble in a repeated reading from the place of the error, they may make do with reading the verse in which the error was, together with another two verses before or after it, and afterwards they should skip and continue reading the aliya at which they are (see Mishna Berura 142:2; Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 3).

If after the end of the Torah reading on Shabbat they concluded that there was an error requiring repetition, by the letter of the law there is no need to go back and read the verse in which the reader erred, for we have learned that some hold that one fulfils the obligation even with a reading that contains an error, and since it is a rabbinic mitzva, the halakha follows the view of the lenient (Ḥayei Adam 31:31; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 142:5). However, if there is no great trouble in it, it is good to go back and read without a blessing the verse in which they erred, together with another two verses before or after it (see Biur Halakha 142:1, s.v. 'Maḥzirin').

sections.title_en: 18. Reading from an Invalid Scroll
sections.body_en:
A kosher Torah scroll is a Torah scroll all of whose letters are written properly, for the sake of Heaven, in ink on parchment. For the whole Torah is one complete divine idea, which is expressed in all the letters of the Torah. And if even one letter is missing or is written in an invalid way – the whole scroll is invalid.

According to most Rishonim, the enactment of the Sages to read the Torah in public must be carried out with a kosher Torah scroll, and in a place where there is no kosher Torah scroll, one should not bless on the reading from an invalid scroll (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh and Mordekhai). And some Rishonim hold that when there is no kosher scroll, one may fulfil the Torah reading with a blessing from an invalid Torah scroll that is written in ink on parchment (Responsa of the Sages of Narbonne, Rambam and Ra'avya).

In practice, when there is no kosher Torah scroll, they should read from the invalid Torah scroll without a blessing (Shulḥan Arukh 143:3; Mishna Berura 143:9. When the defect is in another ḥumash – it is explained in the note).18

notes_en.en:
Gittin (60a): "Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: A Torah scroll that is missing one sheet – one does not read from it". And further there: "Rabba and Rav Yosef both said: One does not read from ḥumashim in the synagogue, because of the honour of the public". So that they will not appear like poor people who do not have a complete Torah scroll (Rashba). And likewise in the Yerushalmi (Megilla 3:1): "Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman in the name of R. Yonatan: A defective Torah – one does not read from it in public", because, out of their sorrow at being unable to read in the Torah, they will obtain a kosher Torah scroll. And so ruled most of the Rishonim, that one should not read from a single ḥumash written on parchment or from an invalid Torah scroll, among them: Sefer Ha-Ora (2:156), Maḥzor Vitry (119), the Ramban (Megilla 17a), the Rashba (Responsa Ha-Ḥadashot 13), the Rosh (Responsa 3:8), the Maharam Ḥalawa (147), the Mordekhai (Gittin 406), the Rashbash (11) and others. And so it emerges from the words of the Rambam (Laws of a Torah Scroll 10:1). On the other hand, the Rambam wrote in his responsa (294) that having no choice one may read with a blessing from a ḥumash written in ink on parchment, or from a Torah scroll invalid because it was not processed properly, for the blessing is on the reading of the Torah and not on the scroll. And he testified that so they were accustomed in the lands of the West, to read from a scroll that was not processed properly, before R. Yosef Migash, the Rif and other sages, and they did not protest against them. And so wrote the Sages of Narbonne (Responsa of the Ba'alei Ha-Tosafot 16). And so wrote the Ra'avya (553) concerning a scroll in which letters are missing (and so it is explained from the Agur in the name of the Maharil, and the Terumat Ha-Deshen in the name of his uncle, brought in the next note). And so wrote the Responsa Maharam of Lublin (84) concerning the reading on Shabbat morning, which is the obligation of the day. And so wrote the Eliya Rabba (143:9). And so wrote Rav Goren (Siddur La-Ḥayal, Laws of the Torah Reading 23) concerning an army camp that has only an invalid Torah scroll. And in the Kesef Mishneh (Torah Scroll 10:1) he explained that the words of the Rambam in his Laws refer to when there is a kosher scroll (and the Rashba, in Ha-Ḥadashot 13, explained that the Rambam wrote the responsum in his youth, and in halakha he was stringent).
When the defect is not in the ḥumash from which one needs to read, some say that even according to those who forbid reading from an invalid scroll, having no choice it is permitted to read from it with a blessing (Rashba, Gittin 60a; Ran on the Rif, Gittin 27b). And some rule so in halakha, since there is a double doubt (sfek sfeika) for leniency: perhaps the halakha follows those who hold that having no choice it is permitted to read from an invalid scroll, and perhaps it follows those who hold that it is permitted when the defect is in another ḥumash. And so ruled in practice the Rema (143:4), the Derisha (1), the Peri Ḥadash (4), the Noda Bi-Yehuda (first edition, Yoreh De'ah 71), the Ḥayei Adam (31:34), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (143:7) and others. On the other hand, some incline to be stringent not to read from it (Sha'arei Efrayim 6:63. And see Beit Me'ir 143 and Biur Halakha 143:4, s.v. 'Yesh').

sections.title_en: 19. An Error Found in the Middle of the Reading
sections.body_en:
If they began to read in the Torah, and in the course of the reading an error was discovered about which there is doubt whether it invalidates the scroll, they should continue to read from the Torah scroll with a blessing and not replace it with another, because of a 'double doubt' (sfek sfeika). First, it is possible that the error found does not invalidate the scroll. Second, even if it invalidates it, some say that after the fact one fulfils the obligation with a reading from an invalid Torah scroll, and since they have already begun to read from this scroll, because of the honour of the scroll, the reading should be finished from it (Rema 143:4; Mishna Berura 25).

But if in the middle of the reading an error was found that certainly invalidates the scroll, a kosher Torah scroll must be taken out of the ark, and the reading continued from it. But there is no need to repeat what was already read, because in this matter one relies on those who hold that after the fact one fulfils the obligation with a reading from an invalid scroll (Rema 143:4; Mishna Berura 13).

If the defect was found in the middle of the reading of one of the people called up, some say that the invalid Torah scroll must be replaced at once with a kosher one, and at least three verses read from the kosher scroll, so that the person called up will recite the final blessing on a reading from a kosher Torah scroll (Shulḥan Arukh 143:4).

And some say that if the reader is at a place where it is possible to end the reading (which is not fewer than three verses before or after a section, above halakha 5), the person called up should recite the final blessing on what he read from the invalid scroll, so as not to change the scrolls in the middle of the aliya. But if the error was found at a place where it is not possible to stop, since one should not continue to read from the invalid scroll, they must change the scrolls and continue the reading from the kosher scroll, and the person called up should recite the final blessing on the kosher scroll (Rema there; Mishna Berura 13).19

In every case where an error was found in the Torah scroll, the gabbaim must see to its correction as soon as possible (above 10:21).

notes_en.en:
As we learned in the previous note, some say that when there is no kosher scroll it is permitted to read from an invalid scroll. And in their view, even if they read in the Torah and discovered that the scroll is invalid, they have fulfilled the obligation, and there is no need to go back and read from a kosher scroll. And according to the Agur (195) in the name of the Maharil, if they began to read from a Torah scroll and found in it an error that invalidates it, they should continue to read from it, for it is possible that the second scroll they take out is also invalid (because of 'missing and extra letters'). And so wrote the Terumat Ha-Deshen (Pesakim U-Khetavim 70) in the name of his uncle R. Aharon Blumlein. And so wrote the Maharal (Tiferet Yisrael 67) and the Leḥem Ḥamudot (Torah Scroll 88). On the other hand, according to most poskim one does not fulfil the obligation with an invalid scroll, and consequently according to their view, even if they already read from the invalid one – a kosher scroll must be taken out and the whole portion read again from it from its beginning with a blessing (Responsa of the Rosh 3:8). And the Kesef Mishneh wrote (Torah Scroll 10:1) in the name of the Mahari Beirav that concerning what was already read from the invalid scroll, one relies on the views that validate the reading from it in a pressing situation, and there is no need to go back and read from a kosher scroll what was read from the invalid scroll.
If the error was found in the middle of the reading, I wrote above the two main views, of the Shulḥan Arukh and the Rema, according to which those of Sephardi and Ashkenazi origin are accustomed. And there is a further view, that even if the error was discovered at a place where it is not possible to stop, they should continue to read from the invalid scroll up to where it is permitted to stop, and bless on it, and only afterwards change the scroll (Mordekhai, Megilla 793-794; Baḥ 143:2; Magen Avraham 4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 5).

sections.title_en: 20. The Law of a Minyan That Missed a Torah Reading
sections.body_en:
If six who prayed individually and did not read the Torah gathered in the morning hours, they may join another four with them and read the Torah. And even if they gathered in the afternoon, they can make up the Torah reading at the time of Minḥa, for although the time of the Torah reading is ideally at the Shaḥarit prayer, after the fact one may read all day (Mishna Berura 135:1). Therefore, a minyan of soldiers or people who were travelling and did not have a Torah scroll at the time of the Shaḥarit prayer, and in the afternoon arrived at a place where there is a Torah scroll, can read in the Torah what they missed at Shaḥarit.20

If something happened that cancelled the minyan on Shabbat, and the public missed the reading of the weekly portion, on the following Shabbat they should make it up and read two portions in the order of their appearance in the Torah (Or Zarua 2:45; Rema 135:2). And if it happened that they missed the Torah reading for several Shabbatot, some say that it is possible to make up only one additional portion, for it was not customary to read more than two portions on one Shabbat (Maharam Mintz 85; Magen Avraham 135:4). And many say that all the portions they missed should be made up (R. Yitzḥak Tyrnau; Eliya Rabba 135:2; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 6). In practice, it is right to make up all the portions, and in the first aliya they should read all the portions that need to be made up, until the end of the first aliya of the portion adjacent to the weekly portion (Petaḥ Ha-Devir 135:4; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 5. But one person called up should not read from two ḥumashim).

One who missed the reading of a portion because he prayed in a community whose order of reading the portions is different, for example he was abroad and Shabbat fell on the second festival day of the Diaspora, and therefore they did not read the weekly portion there – need not make up the Torah reading, for the obligation of the reading rests on the public and not on the individual (Halikhot Shlomo, Prayer 12:6; Ḥazon Ovadia, Shabbat 2, p. 332). (The obligation that rests on the individual is to read the portion shenayim mikra ve-eḥad targum, as explained in Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 5:9-10.)

notes_en.en:
Some say that there must be ten who did not hear the Torah reading, because the Torah reading is not an obligation of the individual but of the public, and as long as there is not a minyan who did not hear, one should not read with a blessing (Binyan Shlomo 1:35; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 69:14). On the other hand, some say that even three who did not hear the Torah reading may join seven with them and read the Torah (Peri Ha-Sadeh 4:90; Torat Yekutiel, Rosenberg 51). And the custom follows the view of most poskim, that as long as there is a majority of a minyan they may make up the Torah reading (Biur Halakha 143:1, s.v. 'Be-faḥot me-asara'; Maharsham 1:175; Ketzot Ha-Shulḥan part 1, 25:14; Har Tzvi, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:52. And according to R. Ḥayim Palagi, Lev Ḥayim 2:25, there must be seven who did not hear).
Some say that in the afternoon it is preferable not to make up the reading, because it is a strange thing (Beit She'arim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 50, and the Yabi'a Omer part 4, Oraḥ Ḥayim 17 inclined to this). However, according to many it is permitted to make up the reading even in the afternoon, and so the Ḥatam Sofer and Rabbi Yehuda Assad conducted themselves (Yehuda Ya'aleh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 51; Goren David 1:5; Melumdei Milḥama 27). And likewise is the law concerning making up the reading on Shabbat in the afternoon (Dagul Me-Revava 135:2; Tzitz Eliezer 13:27).
